rationale: SciCoQA 41c16fd1 (reported): The paper describes a flow-matching training loss that predicts clean translations and rotations at time t and penalizes squared errors with a normalization factor of 1/(1 − t). In the code, the implementation first divides the translation and rotation errors by (1 − t) (with clipping) and then squares them, i.e., it computes ((error)/(1 − t))^2. rationale: SciCoQA a17a3073 (reported): The paper states that the input sequence to the model is ordered as non-predicted tokens, followed by mask tokens, and then predicted tokens, denoted as `(x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}, x_{z>c})`. In the official code, however, the `MaskedDataset` collator appends two sets of mask tokens to the end of the full permuted sequence `[x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}]`, creating an intermediate sequence structured as `[x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}, M_{z>c}, M_{z>c}]`. The model's forwarding logic subsequently splits the last set of mask tokens into the query stream and retains `[x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}, M_{z>c}]` as the input for the content stream, differing from the order specified in the paper.

evidence.text: Additionally, we add mask tokens M_{z>c} right before the predicted part, and obtain the new input tokens (x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}, x_{z>c}) = (x_1, x_3, x_5, [M], [M], [M], x_4, x_6, x_2) and the corresponding position sequence (p_1, p_3, p_5, p_4, p_6, p_2, p_4, p_6, p_2), as shown in Figure 2a. In MPNet, (x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}) are taken as the non-predicted part, and x_{z>c} = (x_4, x_6, x_2) are taken as the predicted part.
Figure 2: (a) The structure of MPNet. ... The predicted part x_{z>c} = (x_4, x_6, x_2) is predicted by the query stream.

note: Verified method discrepancy: paper specifies input ordering (x_{z<=c}, M_{z>c}, x_{z>c}), whereas official repository MaskedDataset collator at pretraining/fairseq/tasks/masked_permutation_lm.py:167 appends masks to the end [x_{z<=c}, x_{z>c}, M_{z>c}], altering the content stream order; confirmed method mismatch.

rationale: SciCoQA a2a366d4 (synthetic): The paper states that at test time the final sentiment output should come from the source-view classifier, due to exposure bias affecting the summary-view classifier. The code, however, saves the merged ensemble of source-view and summary-view sentiment predictions as the primary output used for evaluation when available. As a result, evaluation in the code reflects an ensemble/merged classifier rather than the source-view classifier specified by the paper.

evidence.text: In the testing stage, we use the sentiment label predicted by the source-view classifier as the final classification prediction. The reason is that the decoder suffers from the well-known exposure bias problem …

note: Verified method discrepancy: paper specifies test-time sentiment evaluated solely from source-view classifier, whereas repository code at predict.py uses an ensemble of source and summary views for evaluation; confirmed method mismatch.

rationale: SciCoQA b20489a8 (synthetic): The paper emphasizes that Confidence Bootstrapping should focus learning on the early reverse-diffusion steps (high-noise regime, large t), and explicitly mentions weighting to give larger emphasis to high noise levels while preventing forgetting for small t. The code’s loss function multiplies all translational/rotational/torsional losses by (1 − t), which increases emphasis on low-noise (late) steps, effectively reversing the intended focus. This directly conflicts with the paper’s stated training emphasis.

evidence.text: Using different λ and λ′ allows us to take advantage of the multiresolution decomposition of diffusion models and direct the bootstrapping feedback principally to update the initial steps of the reverse diffusion.” (Section 4.3)

During fine-tuning we use λ′(t)=1/(2μt^2) and λ′(t)=t/μt^2, to give more emphasis to the bootstrapping examples at high noise levels… We … give [training samples] a larger weight for small t.” (Appendix C.1)

note: Verified method discrepancy: paper specifies weighting emphasizing early high-noise reverse diffusion steps (large t), whereas repository code at utils/training.py multiplies losses by (1-t), reversing emphasis to low-noise steps; confirmed method mismatch.

rationale: SciCoQA b42305a7 (synthetic): The paper uses fixed noise schedules (geometric and log-linear) and notes it did not systematically explore noise schedules beyond these. The code makes the log-linear schedule’s epsilon a learnable parameter, turning the schedule into a trainable component. This introduces a modeling choice not discussed in the paper and changes the training dynamics away from the fixed-schedule assumption.

evidence.text: We tested a geometric noise schedule (that interpolates between 10^{-5} and 20), as well as a log-linear noise schedule … Outside of this, we did not systemically explore noise schedules or alternative loss weightings, although these could likely improve generation quality.
For each p_{t|0}^{tok}(·|·), we … set Q_t^{tok} = σ(t) Q^{tok} … define σ̄(t) as the cumulative noise ∫_0^t σ(s) ds …

note: Verified method discrepancy: paper specifies fixed geometric and log-linear noise schedules, whereas repository code at noise_lib.py makes the log-linear schedule epsilon parameter learnable; confirmed method mismatch.

rationale: SciCoQA c88fe9fb (synthetic): The paper states the use of cosine similarity for S(i, j), implying that embeddings are L2-normalized before similarity computation. In the code, the final aggregated image and text embeddings are left unnormalized, and the similarity is computed as a raw dot product, which depends on vector magnitudes. This deviates from the cosine similarity assumption and changes both the loss behavior and retrieval scoring.

evidence.text: S(i, j) is the similarity function between image and caption features. We used the standard cosine similarity as S(·, ·).

note: Verified method discrepancy: paper specifies cosine similarity S(i,j) with L2-normalized embeddings, whereas repository code at models/tern.py computes raw dot product without normalizing image and caption embeddings; confirmed method mismatch.

rationale: SciCoQA ec9f2402 (synthetic): The paper states that the shift equivariance of the feature extractor is ensured by using circular padding before each convolution to preserve timing information exactly. In the code, the SincNet backbone applies standard zero (constant) padding before each convolutional layer. This breaks the exact shift equivariance property that the paper relies on for theoretical guarantees, creating a direct mismatch between the described method and the implementation.

evidence.text: Although CNNs are generally approximately shift-equivariant, not all implementations satisfy this property exactly, due to edge effects. We therefore employ circular padding of the signals before each convolutional layer in the network in order to preserve the timing information completely.

Definition 2.1. Let x be a signal and (x)τ denote a column-wise circular shift of x. Then f: RN → RN×L is said to be equivariant with respect to time shifts if for any time lag τ ∈ Z we have that f((x)τ) = (f(x))τ.

note: Verified method discrepancy: paper specifies circular padding in SincNet convolutions to preserve shift-equivariance, whereas repository code at dnn_models.py applies constant zero padding; confirmed method mismatch.
